sections.b:
2 Samuel 1–10 tells how David became king of all Israel without, the narrator insists, lifting a hand against Saul's house. He mourns Saul and Jonathan (1:17–27), is anointed king of Judah at Hebron (2:4), and waits through a long civil war while Saul's house collapses: Abner is murdered by Joab (3:27), Ish-bosheth by his own captains (4:5–7), and David punishes the killers each time. The elders of all Israel anoint him at Hebron (5:3). He takes Jerusalem, brings the ark there with dancing (6), receives God's promise of a lasting house (7), wins wars on every side (8; 10), and seats Jonathan's lame son at his table (9). The section ends with David at the height of his power, ruling "with justice and righteousness" (8:15), just before his fall in chapter 11.

A widely held critical view reads 2 Samuel 1–5 as royal apology, a defense written to clear David of suspected involvement in the deaths of Saul, Abner and Ish-bosheth (P. Kyle McCarter, James VanderKam, Baruch Halpern, Steven McKenzie). Traditional readers take the narrator's account of David's innocence at face value.

common: David became king by waiting for God's timing instead of seizing power.

sections.b: After Gilboa, Saul's house survives for a few years east of the Jordan. Abner makes Saul's son Ish-bosheth king at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 2:8–10), but the house grows weaker (2 Samuel 3:1). Abner defects and is killed (2 Samuel 3), Ish-bosheth is murdered in his bed (2 Samuel 4), and Saul's daughter Michal, taken back by David, dies childless (2 Samuel 6:23). David honors Saul in his lament (2 Samuel 1:19–27), thanks the men of Jabesh for burying him (2 Samuel 2:5–7), and keeps faith with Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9).
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 1:19–27; 2 Samuel 2:8–10; 2 Samuel 3:1; 2 Samuel 4:1–12; 2 Samuel 6:23; 2 Samuel 9:1–13

sections.b: David's song for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:19–27) praises them together, "never torn apart" in life or death, and then turns to Jonathan alone: "You were a great delight to me. Your love was a wonder to me, more than the love of women" (2 Samuel 1:26). David later keeps his oath to Jonathan by restoring Saul's land to Jonathan's son Mephibosheth and giving him a place at the king's table (2 Samuel 9:1–13; compare 1 Samuel 20:14–17).

As the price of his covenant with Abner, David demands the return of Michal, whom Saul had given to Paltiel (2 Samuel 3:13–16). She is taken from her weeping husband without a word recorded from her. When the ark comes to Jerusalem she watches David dance from a window, "felt contempt for him" (2 Samuel 6:16), and mocks him for exposing himself. David answers that God chose him over her father (2 Samuel 6:21), and the chapter ends: Michal had no child to the day of her death (2 Samuel 6:23). Readers have seen in her a woman used by both her father and her husband.

common: Michal was punished with childlessness for despising David's worship.
uncommon: The Talmud identifies Michal with Eglah, mother of David's son Ithream, and says she died giving birth (Bavli Sanhedrin 21a).

sections.b: David brings the ark from Kiriath-jearim, where it had stayed since its return from the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:1–2). The first attempt, on a new cart, ends when Uzzah touches the ark and dies (2 Samuel 6:6–7). After three months of blessing on the house of Obed-edom, the ark is carried up with sacrifices, dancing and the ram's horn, and set in a tent David pitched in the City of David (2 Samuel 6:12–17). Chronicles adds that the Levites now carried it on poles as Moses had commanded (1 Chronicles 15:2, 15:13–15). The ark's arrival makes Jerusalem the place of God's throne and leads directly to David's wish to build a temple (2 Samuel 7:2).

common: Uzzah died because the ark was moved in a way the law forbade.

sections.b: Jerusalem was a Jebusite city that neither Judah nor Benjamin had taken (Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21). David captures "Zion's fortress" and names it the City of David (2 Samuel 5:6–9), probably by way of the water shaft or channel (tsinnor) whose meaning is debated (2 Samuel 5:8). He builds there, Hiram of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen (2 Samuel 5:11), and David brings the ark into the city (2 Samuel 6). On the border of Judah and Benjamin and belonging to neither, it became a capital for all Israel.

The name Zion first appears in the Bible when David takes "Zion's fortress" from the Jebusites (2 Samuel 5:7). At first it names the citadel on the narrow southeastern ridge of Jerusalem, above the Gihon spring. With the ark brought there (2 Samuel 6) and later the temple built just north of it, the name spreads to the temple hill and the whole city.

sections.h: David's kingship: covenant, shepherd and ruler
sections.b: David's rise shows the book's view of a rightful king. God chose him as nagid, "ruler" (2 Samuel 5:2; 2 Samuel 6:21; 2 Samuel 7:8), and the people made him melekh, "king," anointing him first over Judah (2 Samuel 2:4) and then over Israel, after he made a covenant with the elders (2 Samuel 5:3). He is the shepherd of God's people (2 Samuel 5:2; 2 Samuel 7:7–8) and rules "with justice and righteousness" (2 Samuel 8:15). Yet the warnings of Deuteronomy's law of the king hover nearby: more wives (2 Samuel 5:13; compare Deuteronomy 17:17) and a kingdom raised "for the good of his people" (2 Samuel 5:12).
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 2:4; 2 Samuel 5:1–3; 2 Samuel 5:12–13; 2 Samuel 6:21; 2 Samuel 7:8; 2 Samuel 8:15; Deuteronomy 17:14–20

sections.b: The hope for a Messiah, an anointed king of David's line, grows from Nathan's oracle (2 Samuel 7:11–16): God will raise up David's offspring, make his throne stand forever, and be a father to him. In 2 Samuel the title "the LORD's anointed" still means the reigning king (2 Samuel 1:14), but the promise of an everlasting throne reached beyond any one king. Psalms and prophets built on it when the dynasty failed, and the New Testament proclaims Jesus as the son of David who receives David's throne (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30).
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 1:14; 2 Samuel 7:11–16; Psalm 89:3–4; Isaiah 9:6–7; Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30

common: The promise of 2 Samuel 7 is the main Old Testament root of the hope for a Messiah, son of David.
uncommon: Some critical scholars think the eternal promise was first royal propaganda for Solomon and only later became a hope for a future king.

sections.b: David answers the promise by sitting before the LORD and praying (2 Samuel 7:18–29). He calls himself "your servant" ten times and addresses God as "Lord GOD" seven times. He marvels that God has spoken "far into the future" (2 Samuel 7:19), praises God's uniqueness and his redemption of Israel (2 Samuel 7:22–24), and asks God to do what he has said, "so that people say, 'The LORD of Armies is God over Israel!'" (2 Samuel 7:26). The prayer turns a promise into a request; later psalms do the same (Psalm 89:49; Psalm 132:10–12).

claude.title: Claude's theory: "house" as the chapter's argument
claude.body: My own reading: 2 Samuel 7 does not just play on the word "house"; it makes an argument with it. David begins with a building (7:2), God answers with a family (7:11), the son links the two by building for God's name (7:13), and David's prayer asks that the family be blessed "for all time" (7:29). The movement from a house of cedar to a house of persons suggests that God values the people more than the building. Scholars have long traced the wordplay; reading it as a deliberate argument about what kind of house God wants is my own suggestion.
claude.refs: 2 Samuel 7:2; 2 Samuel 7:5; 2 Samuel 7:11; 2 Samuel 7:13; 2 Samuel 7:16; 2 Samuel 7:29

sections.b: Once the ark is in Jerusalem, David wants to build God a house of cedar (2 Samuel 7:1–3). God refuses: he has never lived in a house or asked for one, and David's son will build it (2 Samuel 7:5–7, 7:13). Chronicles adds that David was a man of war who had shed much blood (1 Chronicles 22:8). David still prepares, dedicating plunder from his wars to the LORD (2 Samuel 8:11), treasure that Solomon later brings into the temple (1 Kings 7:51).

sections.h: Loyal love in David's early reign
sections.b: Hesed, loyal love, is a key word in 2 Samuel 2–10. David blesses the men of Jabesh for their hesed to Saul (2 Samuel 2:5–6). Abner claims to have shown hesed to Saul's house (2 Samuel 3:8). God promises that his hesed will never leave David's son as it left Saul (2 Samuel 7:15). David shows "the loyal love of God" to Jonathan's son (2 Samuel 9:1, 9:3, 9:7) and tries to show it to Hanun of Ammon, who repays it with insult (2 Samuel 10:2).

David is anointed three times: by Samuel in private (1 Samuel 16:13), by the men of Judah at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:4), and by the elders of all Israel at Hebron after a covenant (2 Samuel 5:3). Between these, David refuses to harm "the LORD's anointed" Saul, and executes the Amalekite who claimed to have done so (2 Samuel 1:14–16). In his lament, Saul's shield lies "with no oil to anoint it" (2 Samuel 1:21).

The Philistines celebrated Saul's death (2 Samuel 1:20), and when David was anointed king of all Israel they came up to hunt him in the Valley of Rephaim (2 Samuel 5:17–18). Twice David asked the LORD and defeated them, carrying off their idols as they had once carried off the ark (2 Samuel 5:19–25). Later he subdued them and took Metheg-ammah (2 Samuel 8:1), and Philistine and Cretan soldiers, the Kerethites and Pelethites, became his bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18).

When Nahash dies, David sends comfort to his son Hanun, who shames the envoys by shaving half their beards and cutting their robes (2 Samuel 10:1–5). Ammon hires Aramean armies, and Joab and Abishai defeat them outside Rabbah (2 Samuel 10:6–14). The war continues into the siege of Rabbah, during which David sins with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:1; 2 Samuel 12:26–31).

Although David's great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite and he had once left his parents in Moab's care (1 Samuel 22:3–4), he treats defeated Moab harshly, killing two-thirds of the prisoners by measuring them with a cord, and makes Moab pay tribute (2 Samuel 8:2). A midrash explains the change by saying Moab had killed David's family (Numbers Rabbah 14:1). Many readers connect it with Balaam's oracle of a scepter that would crush Moab (Numbers 24:17).

David defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt, eighteen thousand men (2 Samuel 8:13, reading Edom with the Greek and Chronicles), sets garrisons throughout the land, and makes the Edomites his servants (2 Samuel 8:14). Chronicles credits the victory to Abishai (1 Chronicles 18:12), and the title of Psalm 60 to Joab. 1 Kings 11:15–16 recalls Joab's slaughter there and an Edomite prince who escaped to Egypt.

David has six sons by six wives at Hebron (2 Samuel 3:2–5) and takes more wives and concubines in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:13–16). Several marriages were alliances, such as with the daughter of the king of Geshur, mother of Absalom. A king's concubines stood for his throne, so Abner's relations with Saul's concubine Rizpah were seen as a claim to power (2 Samuel 3:7). Deuteronomy had warned that a king must not take many wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), and the rivalries among David's sons fill the chapters that follow.

David himself takes a priestly role in bringing the ark to Jerusalem, wearing a linen ephod, offering sacrifices and blessing the people (2 Samuel 6:14–18). His officials include the priests Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar (2 Samuel 8:17), and, surprisingly, "David's sons served as priests" (2 Samuel 8:18), which Chronicles changes to "first in rank beside the king" (1 Chronicles 18:17). Zadok's origin is debated: Chronicles traces him to Aaron (1 Chronicles 6:4–8), while some scholars think he was Jerusalem's Jebusite priest.

When Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark and is struck dead (2 Samuel 6:6–7), the story shows the danger of handling the holy carelessly. The law said that even the Levites who carried the ark must not touch the holy things or they would die (Numbers 4:15). The same ark brings blessing to Obed-edom's house (2 Samuel 6:11), and David learns to carry it rightly (1 Chronicles 15:13–15).

As the ark sets out, David and all Israel make merry before the LORD "with all their strength and with songs, with lyres, harps, hand drums, rattles and cymbals" (2 Samuel 6:5). When it comes up to Jerusalem, David whirls before the LORD with all his strength, amid shouts and the ram's horn (2 Samuel 6:14–15). David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:19–27) shows the other side of Israel's music, the song of grief.

sections.h: David's laments for Saul, Jonathan and Abner
sections.b: David sings two laments in these chapters. "The Bow" (2 Samuel 1:19–27), taken from the Book of Jashar, mourns Saul and Jonathan with the refrain "How the warriors have fallen!" and never mentions God or Saul's sins. The short lament for Abner (2 Samuel 3:33–34) asks why he died like a fool, though his hands were not tied. Both serve as public grief and as statements of David's innocence. David will lament again over Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33).

Hebron was a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7). There Joab kills Abner in the gate to avenge his brother Asahel, whom Abner had killed in battle after warning him twice (2 Samuel 2:18–23; 2 Samuel 3:27). By the law of refuge Abner was not a murderer. David declares himself innocent and curses Joab's house (2 Samuel 3:28–29), and on his deathbed he names Joab's guilt (1 Kings 2:5).

sections.h: The Dead Sea scroll of Samuel in 2 Samuel 1–10
sections.b: The scroll 4QSam-a, copied about 50–25 BC, often agrees with the Greek or with Chronicles against the Masoretic Text. In 2 Samuel 1–10 it lacks the summary of David's reign (2 Samuel 5:4–5); names the place where the ark was kept, "Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim" (2 Samuel 6:2); reads "with all strength and with songs" for the Masoretic "with all cypress woods" (2 Samuel 6:5); lacks a repeated line in 2 Samuel 6:3–4; is reported (Ulrich; DJD 17) to have seven bulls and seven rams in place of an ox and a calf (2 Samuel 6:13); and preserves "a thousand chariots" (2 Samuel 8:4) and an added note about Shishak (2 Samuel 8:7). The Greek also preserves a better text at 2 Samuel 4:6. Comparing these witnesses with Chronicles shows that the Chronicler used a Samuel text close to the scroll.
sections.refs: 2 Samuel 4:6; 2 Samuel 5:4–5; 2 Samuel 6:2–13; 2 Samuel 8:4–8; 1 Chronicles 13:6–10; 1 Chronicles 18:4

sections.b: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan is "written in the Book of Jashar" (2 Samuel 1:18), the same lost collection that preserved Joshua's words to the sun (Joshua 10:13). It was probably a book of old war songs and poems. Later works called the Book of Jasher are not the ancient book.

In 2 Samuel 1–10 Joab leads David's men against Abner at Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:12–32), murders Abner to avenge Asahel (2 Samuel 3:22–30), is named commander of the army (2 Samuel 8:16), and leads the war against Ammon and Aram, telling Abishai, "Be strong... The LORD will do whatever he sees is good" (2 Samuel 10:12). David complains that the sons of Zeruiah are too harsh for him (2 Samuel 3:39).
David's first act as king of Judah is to bless the men of Jabesh-gilead for their loyal love in burying Saul, and to invite them to accept him as king (2 Samuel 2:4–7).

sections.h: "The LORD of Armies" and "Lord GOD" in 2 Samuel
sections.b: 2 Samuel uses the title "the LORD of Armies" for the God who goes before David's armies (2 Samuel 5:10; 2 Samuel 5:24) and who is enthroned on the cherubim above the ark (2 Samuel 6:2, 6:18). In David's prayer the title "Lord GOD" (Adonai YHWH) appears seven times (2 Samuel 7:18–29), and David prays that people will say, "The LORD of Armies is God over Israel" (2 Samuel 7:26).
